lines.text: Every Solana program can be changed by someone. The question is who, and how fast.
Right now, seven hundred sixty-nine million dollars sits behind programs that can be upgraded with no waiting period.
How safe is your money? It comes down to two things: who must agree to a change, and how long you get to leave.
Keyholder puts every program on one of four stages. One key. A few keys, but no wait. Keys and a waiting period. Or it can't be changed at all.
Here are all five hundred seventy-seven. The taller the column, the more money it holds. Pick one, and its signer keys fan out.
Kamino Lend waits a day before an upgrade. But its admin key, four of ten signers, can act at once. The weakest path sets the stage.
And keys are shared. This one sits on six multisigs, behind one and a half billion dollars, and two of them need only its signature.
Some changes are already waiting. Fifty-three open votes could change who controls a program. One was approved seven hundred days ago, and it can still run.
You don't need to read code to check any of this. Ask in plain words, and the answer comes straight from the record.
Would it have mattered? We replayed the Drift hack from the chain. Keyholder's rules flag the first control change five and a half days before two hundred eighty-five million dollars moved.
And programs can act on it. One line, require stage, refuses a deposit when the target's control is too weak. On devnet, it refused a real one, twenty-three seconds after a multisig was weakened.
We hold ourselves to the same rule. Keyholder's own program only changes through two of three keys, after forty-eight hours in public.
Who can move it, how fast, and did that change? That's Keyholder.
